name: Brown pelican
in_book: Bertha and Oscar; the hooked pelican Snapper carries to the door; the fish-head thief at Lostman's.
facts: Dive from 30–60 feet and hit the water head-first; air sacs under the skin cushion the impact.
A pouch can hold about three gallons — more than the stomach.
Nearly wiped out in the 1960s–70s by DDT; recovered and delisted in 2009.
Fishing line and hooks are now one of their biggest killers — exactly the rescue Dan performs.

name: Bottlenose dolphin
in_book: The playful pair at Lopez River; the mother who rams the hammerhead and bites her calf free of the net.
facts: Everglades dolphins live in small resident groups and work the mangrove edges in teams.
Mothers really do defend calves aggressively, and dolphins have been documented ramming sharks.
Abandoned 'ghost' nets are a leading cause of dolphin and sea-turtle entanglement.

name: American alligator
in_book: The marina gators tourists get too close to; the grouper thief at Lostman's; Alligator Alley; the poachers who caused Dad's death.
facts: Everglades gators tolerate brackish water near river mouths but prefer fresh.
Splashing attracts them — Matt's rule about not splashing is real guide wisdom.
Poaching for hides was once rampant; legal protection since 1967 brought them back.

name: Cottonmouth (water moccasin)
in_book: The snake drawn to the lantern at Comer Key.
facts: Florida cottonmouths swim with the whole body on the surface; harmless water snakes swim with just the head up.
The white mouth gape is a warning, not an attack.
Bites are serious but rarely fatal with treatment — which is why 'a long time to a mainland hospital' matters.

name: Sharks of the Ten Thousand Islands
in_book: The 'Mako' on the beach at Comer Key; the hammerhead at the ghost net.
facts: Bull sharks are the shallow-water shark of the Everglades and move far up the rivers.
Shortfin makos are open-ocean fish; the Comer Key shark was more likely a bull — a nice discussion point.
Great hammerheads cruise the passes hunting tarpon during the spring migration.

name: Mangroves
in_book: Everywhere. The hideout at Pavilion Key, the storm tie-off, the overhangs where snook wait.
facts: Red mangroves' prop roots are a fish nursery — most of the fish in this book start life there.
The Ten Thousand Islands is one of the largest mangrove forests in the world.
'Every mangrove key and bay looked alike' — guides navigate by chart, memory, and tide.

name: Oyster bars
in_book: The thing that scrapes the hull, holds the Sea Belle, cuts your line, and hides the redfish.
facts: Oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day each.
Bars grow at river mouths where fresh and salt water mix — the same place the fish gather.
Wading boots like Snapper's are essential; shells cut like glass.

name: Bald cypress
in_book: 'Colossal cypress trees gnarled up out of the ground like giant twisted guardians of the realm' on the drive in.
facts: Deciduous conifers; the 'knees' may help with stability in soft mud.
The Fakahatchee Strand along the Everglades City road is the largest cypress strand in the world.

name: Banyan / strangler fig
in_book: Two massive banyans flank Dan's front yard.

name: Mosquitoes, sand fleas, no-see-ums
in_book: 'It was the mosquitos that chomped at his peace of mind.' Dan's homemade lavender repellent.
facts: The black salt-marsh mosquito breeds in the mangroves by the billion after rain.
A westerly breeze is the only real relief — which is why Dan picks windy nights to camp.

name: Abandoned fishing nets
in_book: Catches Matt's foot in the storm and the baby dolphin the next day.
facts: Derelict gear keeps 'fishing' for years.
Everglades National Park banned commercial netting in 1985; old nets still turn up.

name: Stone crab
in_book: Matt begging claws from the seafood company as a kid.
facts: Only one claw is taken and the crab is returned alive to regrow it.
Chokoloskee and Everglades City are the stone-crab capital of Florida.

name: Seagrass beds
in_book: Rabbit Key's grass beds — 'grass bed fishing meant trout.'

name: The Everglades choir
in_book: Mullet splashing, frogs croaking, birds singing — Ch. 15's night on deck.

name: Green iguana (invasive)
in_book: Smuggled exotics in the Gazette article.

name: Gull
in_book: Matt's confidant about the lavender repellent.

name: Birds of the islands
in_book: 'Birds danced alongside in the air, no doubt singing songs of Matt's adventures.'
